item.title: Selective Permeability of Protein-Free Phospholipid Vesicles
item.stimulus:
Students made artificial vesicles whose membranes were pure phospholipid bilayers with no embedded proteins. Each batch of vesicles was placed in a solution containing one test substance. After 10 minutes, the students measured the concentration of the substance inside the vesicles as a percentage of its concentration outside. A value of 100% would mean the inside and outside concentrations had become equal.

Substance | Molecular properties | Molecular mass (g/mol) | Inside concentration after 10 min (% of outside)
O₂ | small, nonpolar | 32 | 98
CO₂ | small, nonpolar | 44 | 97
NH₃ (ammonia) | small, polar, uncharged | 17 | 35
Na⁺ | small ion (charged) | 23 | 0.5
Glucose | large, polar | 180 | 2

In a separate trial, the students placed protein-free vesicles containing a concentrated sucrose solution, and also living plant leaf cells, into distilled water. After several hours, many vesicles had burst, but the plant cells had swollen without bursting.
item.model_answer:
(a) The interior of the phospholipid bilayer is made of nonpolar, hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails. O₂ is small and nonpolar, so it can move freely through this hydrophobic region and reached 98% of the outside concentration. Na⁺ is a charged ion, and the nonpolar tails prevent ions from crossing, so with no channel proteins present it reached only 0.5%.

(b) The data do not support the claim. Na⁺ (23 g/mol) is much smaller than glucose (180 g/mol), yet it reached only 0.5% inside, even less than glucose. Also, NH₃ (17 g/mol) is smaller than O₂ (32 g/mol) but reached only 35% compared with 98% for O₂. These results show that charge and polarity, not just size, determine how easily a substance crosses the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer.

(c) The inside glucose concentration will be higher than 2%, moving toward the outside concentration. Glucose is large and polar, so it cannot pass through the hydrophobic tails of the bilayer on its own. Transport proteins embedded in the membrane provide a hydrophilic pathway, so glucose can move through the protein down its concentration gradient from outside (high) to inside (low).

(d) Water entered both the vesicles and the plant cells by osmosis because distilled water is hypotonic to their contents. The vesicles have only a membrane, so they swelled until they burst. The plant cells are surrounded by a rigid cell wall that acts as a structural boundary; as the cell swells, the wall resists further expansion and protects the cell from osmotic lysis.
item.verification_python:
masses={'O2':32,'CO2':44,'NH3':17,'Na':23,'glucose':180}
pct={'O2':98,'CO2':97,'NH3':35,'Na':0.5,'glucose':2}
assert masses['Na']<masses['glucose'] and pct['Na']<pct['glucose']
assert masses['NH3']<masses['O2'] and pct['NH3']<pct['O2']
assert pct['O2']>pct['Na']
assert abs(2*16-32)<1e-9 and abs(12+2*16-44)<1e-9 and abs(14+3-17)<1e-9 and abs(6*12+12+6*16-180)<1e-9
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Permeability of Protein-Free Phospholipid Vesicles
item.stimulus:
A student prepares artificial vesicles whose membranes are pure phospholipid bilayers with no embedded proteins. The student measures how quickly each of four substances crosses the vesicle membrane when it is added at the same concentration to the solution outside the vesicles. Rates are reported in the same arbitrary units for every substance.

Substance | Description | Relative rate of crossing the protein-free bilayer
O₂ | small, nonpolar | 5000
H₂O | small, polar, uncharged | 50
Glucose | large, polar | 0.05
K⁺ | ion (charged) | below detection (less than 0.0001)
item.model_answer:
(a) O₂ rate ÷ H₂O rate = 5000 ÷ 50 = 100, so O₂ crosses 100 times faster than H₂O. The interior of the bilayer is made of the nonpolar hydrocarbon tails of phospholipids, so it is hydrophobic. Small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ pass freely through this nonpolar region. Water is small and uncharged but polar, so the hydrophobic interior restricts it and only small amounts pass through.

(b) K⁺ is an ion with a charge. The nonpolar hydrocarbon tails in the middle of the bilayer prevent ions from crossing, so even though K⁺ is small, its charge keeps it from moving through the hydrophobic interior. Charge matters more than size here.

(c) The rate of K⁺ crossing will increase and become detectable in the vesicles with K⁺ channel proteins. The embedded channel proteins provide a hydrophilic passage through the membrane, so the charged ions can cross without moving through the hydrophobic tails.

(d) The cells whose walls were removed are more likely to burst. As water enters, the cell swells. The cell wall is a rigid structural boundary around the plasma membrane that resists this expansion, which protects walled cells from osmotic lysis. Cells without walls have no such protection.
item.verification_python:
from fractions import Fraction
o2 = Fraction(5000)
h2o = Fraction(50)
glucose = Fraction(5, 100)
ratio = o2 / h2o
assert ratio == 100
# ordering consistent with membrane permeability principles
assert o2 > h2o > glucose > Fraction(1, 10000)
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Solute Passage Across Protein-Free Phospholipid Vesicles
item.stimulus:
A student prepares artificial vesicles made only of a phospholipid bilayer, with no embedded proteins. The vesicles are placed in solutions containing one test substance at a time, and the rate at which each substance enters the vesicles is measured at 25°C. All solutions start at the same concentration of test substance, and the vesicles start with none inside. The results are shown below (relative rates are hypothetical, in arbitrary units; a higher number means faster entry).

Substance | Molecular mass (g/mol) | Polarity or charge | Relative rate of entry
O₂ | 32 | nonpolar | 950
CO₂ | 44 | nonpolar | 900
NH₃ (ammonia) | 17 | polar, uncharged | 30
H₂O | 18 | polar, uncharged | 20
Glucose | 180 | polar, uncharged | less than 0.01
Na⁺ | 23 | charged ion | less than 0.0001
item.model_answer:
(a) O₂ (rate 950) and CO₂ (rate 900) entered fastest. Both are small nonpolar molecules, so they can dissolve into and pass directly through the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer.

(b) Na⁺ is a charged ion and is hydrophilic. The interior of the bilayer is made of the nonpolar hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids, which form a hydrophobic barrier that charged particles cannot pass through, so Na⁺ barely enters even though it is small.

(c) The data do not support the hypothesis. H₂O (18 g/mol) enters at a rate of only 20 and NH₃ (17 g/mol) at 30, while the heavier CO₂ (44 g/mol) enters at 900. Na⁺ (23 g/mol) barely enters at all, while O₂ (32 g/mol) enters at 950. Lighter substances that are polar or charged cross more slowly than heavier nonpolar ones, so polarity and charge, not mass alone, determine how quickly a substance crosses the bilayer.

(d) Glucose will enter faster in the vesicles with glucose transport proteins than in the protein-free vesicles. Glucose is a large polar molecule, so the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails block it from crossing the bilayer directly. The embedded transport protein provides a hydrophilic pathway across the membrane, letting glucose move into the vesicles down its concentration gradient.

item.title: Permeability of Artificial Vesicles to Different Solutes
item.stimulus:
A student prepares two types of artificial vesicles, which are small spheres of membrane enclosing a solution. Type 1 vesicles are made only of phospholipids. Type 2 vesicles are made of the same phospholipids but also contain an embedded potassium channel protein. The student places each vesicle type in separate solutions containing one test substance and measures how far the substance has moved toward equal concentration inside and outside the vesicles after 60 seconds. 100 percent means the inside and outside concentrations have become equal.

Percent of equilibrium reached after 60 seconds
Substance | Type 1 (phospholipid only) | Type 2 (phospholipid + K⁺ channel)
O₂ | 100 | 100
H₂O | 35 | 35
K⁺ | 0.2 | 94
Glucose | 0.4 | 0.4
item.model_answer:
(a) O₂ is a small, nonpolar molecule. The interior of the phospholipid bilayer is hydrophobic, made of nonpolar hydrocarbon tails, so O₂ can diffuse directly through it without needing a channel or transport protein. That is why it reaches 100 percent equilibrium even in Type 1 vesicles.

(b) K⁺ is a charged ion. The nonpolar hydrocarbon tails in the middle of the bilayer block the movement of ions, so with no channel present K⁺ barely crosses (0.2 percent). H₂O is polar, but it is small and uncharged, so it can pass through the bilayer in small amounts, giving the moderate value of 35 percent.

(c) 94 ÷ 0.2 = 470. K⁺ reached a percent of equilibrium 470 times greater in Type 2 vesicles than in Type 1 vesicles.

(d) The hypothesis is not supported. Glucose, a large polar (hydrophilic) molecule, reached 0.4 percent in both vesicle types, and water stayed at 35 percent in both. Only K⁺ increased, from 0.2 to 94 percent. The channel protein increases permeability only to K⁺, not to all hydrophilic substances, so the hypothesis should be rejected.

from fractions import Fraction

k2 = Fraction(94)
ratio = k2 / k1
assert ratio == 470
glc1 = Fraction(4,10); glc2 = Fraction(4,10)
assert glc1 == glc2
h1 = 35; h2 = 35
assert h1 == h2
assert k2 > k1
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Permeability of Artificial Vesicles to Different Solutes
item.stimulus:
Students made two types of artificial vesicles, which are tiny spheres enclosed by a membrane. Type 1 vesicles have a membrane made only of a phospholipid bilayer, with no proteins. Type 2 vesicles have the same phospholipid bilayer plus embedded channel proteins that are specific for potassium ions (K⁺). Each type of vesicle was placed in separate solutions containing one test substance. After 10 minutes the students measured the concentration of the substance inside the vesicles and expressed it as a percentage of the concentration outside. A value of 100% means the inside and outside concentrations are equal. Each value is the mean of five trials.

Substance | Type 1: bilayer only (%) | Type 2: bilayer + K⁺ channels (%)
Oxygen (O₂) | 99 | 99
Ammonia (NH₃) | 40 | 40
Glucose | 2 | 2
Potassium ion (K⁺) | 1 | 95
item.model_answer:
(a) O₂ is a small nonpolar molecule, so it dissolves through the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and crosses freely, reaching 99%. NH₃ is small but polar. The nonpolar hydrocarbon tails in the middle of the bilayer hinder polar molecules, so NH₃ passes only in small amounts and reached just 40% in the same time.

(b) K⁺ is a charged ion, so it is hydrophilic. The nonpolar hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids block ions from crossing the bilayer, which is why K⁺ reached only 1% in Type 1 vesicles. In Type 2 vesicles, the embedded K⁺ channel proteins form a hydrophilic pathway through the membrane. K⁺ can move through this pathway down its concentration gradient without contacting the hydrophobic interior, so it reached 95%.

(c) The data do not support the hypothesis. Glucose, a large polar molecule, reached 2% in both vesicle types. NH₃ reached 40% in both. Adding the channels increased only K⁺ (from 1% to 95%), which shows that the channels are specific to K⁺ and do not raise permeability to all hydrophilic substances.

(d) The wall-less cells are more likely to burst. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water moves into both kinds of cells by osmosis. In intact cells, the cell wall is a rigid structural boundary that resists expansion and protects the cell from osmotic lysis. Without the wall, nothing resists the swelling, so the membrane stretches until the cell bursts.
item.verification_python:
t1={'O2':99,'NH3':40,'glucose':2,'K':1}
t2={'O2':99,'NH3':40,'glucose':2,'K':95}
assert t1['O2']>t1['NH3']
assert t1['K']==1 and t2['K']==95
assert t1['glucose']==t2['glucose']==2
assert t1['NH3']==t2['NH3']==40
assert t2['K']-t1['K']==94
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Using the Type 1 data, explain why O₂ reached a higher percentage than NH₃ after 10 minutes. Both molecules are small; O₂ is nonpolar and NH₃ is polar but uncharged.

criteria.text: Explains that nonpolar O₂ passes freely through the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer, while polar NH₃ crosses it only in small amounts.
criteria.evidence: Response links O₂'s nonpolarity to free passage through the hydrophobic (nonpolar) interior of the bilayer. It also states that NH₃'s polarity limits its passage, so only a small amount crosses.
criteria.fix: Compare each molecule's polarity with the hydrophobic membrane interior: nonpolar molecules dissolve through it freely, while small polar molecules cross only slowly.
accepted_variants: O₂ is nonpolar so it moves easily through the hydrophobic fatty acid tails; NH₃ is polar so the nonpolar tails slow its movement
the nonpolar core lets O₂ through freely but restricts polar NH₃ to small amounts

parts.prompt: Explain why K⁺ reached only 1% in Type 1 vesicles but 95% in Type 2 vesicles.

criteria.text: Explains that K⁺ is charged (hydrophilic), so the nonpolar hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids block it from crossing the bilayer alone.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies K⁺ as an ion, or as charged or hydrophilic. It states that the hydrophobic interior or the nonpolar tails prevent K⁺ from passing through the bilayer.
criteria.fix: State the charge of the ion, then explain that charged particles cannot pass through the nonpolar hydrocarbon tails in the middle of the bilayer.
accepted_variants: ions cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the membrane
the charged K⁺ is repelled by the nonpolar fatty acid tails

criteria.text: Explains that the embedded K⁺ channel proteins provide a hydrophilic pathway through the membrane, so K⁺ can cross.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the channel proteins in Type 2 vesicles let K⁺ pass through the membrane. It describes this route as a hydrophilic pathway or pore that bypasses the hydrophobic interior.
criteria.fix: Describe how an embedded channel protein forms a hydrophilic passage across the membrane that lets a specific ion avoid the hydrophobic interior.
accepted_variants: channel proteins form a pore that lets K⁺ move across without contacting the hydrophobic tails
the channels allow facilitated diffusion of K⁺ across the membrane

parts.prompt: A student hypothesizes that adding K⁺ channel proteins to a membrane increases the membrane's permeability to all hydrophilic substances. Use the data to evaluate this hypothesis.

criteria.text: States that the data do not support the hypothesis, citing glucose (2% in both vesicle types) and/or NH₃ (40% in both) as unchanged when channels were added.
criteria.evidence: Response makes a claim that the hypothesis is not supported, is rejected, or is incorrect. It cites specific data showing that a hydrophilic substance other than K⁺ did not increase with channels: glucose stayed at 2%, or NH₃ stayed at 40%.
criteria.fix: Compare the two columns for each hydrophilic substance other than K⁺, then state whether the values changed and quote the numbers.
accepted_variants: not supported; glucose was 2% with and without channels, so the channels are specific to K⁺
rejected because NH₃ stayed at 40% and glucose at 2% in both vesicle types

parts.prompt: Researchers use enzymes to remove the cell walls from some plant cells. They place intact plant cells and wall-less plant cells in distilled water. Predict which cells are more likely to burst, and justify your prediction.

criteria.text: Predicts that the wall-less cells are more likely to burst, justified by water entering by osmosis and the cell wall providing a structural boundary that protects against osmotic lysis.
criteria.evidence: Response predicts that the wall-less cells burst while the intact cells do not. The justification states that water moves into the cells from the hypotonic distilled water. It also states that the cell wall resists expansion and protects against osmotic lysis, so cells without it cannot resist the swelling.
criteria.fix: Identify the direction of water movement in distilled water, then explain that the cell wall is the structural boundary that resists swelling and lysis.
accepted_variants: the protoplasts burst because water rushes in and nothing resists the expanding membrane, while the wall of intact cells prevents lysis
cells without walls lyse; the wall pushes back against the swelling cell and prevents osmotic lysis

Also, the 95% K⁺ result needs an unstated charge-balancing condition; uncompensated K⁺ entry creates a membrane potential that opposes further entry.

rubric_points: Part (d), d1: The evidence demands that wall-less cells burst and intact cells do not, although the question asks only which are more likely to burst. This can reject a correct probabilistic prediction. The accepted variant 'cells without walls lyse' also lacks the requested justification. accurate: Part (b), b1: The accepted statement that charged K⁺ is 'repelled by the nonpolar fatty acid tails' incorrectly describes the barrier as repulsion. Ion passage through the hydrophobic interior is energetically unfavorable; the nonpolar tails do not electrostatically repel K⁺.

solution: The independent solution agrees with the intended biological conclusions. However, d1's evidence requires certain bursting/nonbursting rather than the defensible relative-likelihood prediction given in the solution. The b1 accepted 'repelled' explanation is not equivalent to the solution's energetically unfavorable crossing explanation. The independent solution also identifies the missing charge-balancing condition needed to interpret the 95% K⁺ result.
first.solve_issues: The intended AP Biology interpretations are answerable from the supplied data. However, the setup does not specify initial internal solute concentrations, pH, or counterion conditions. A physically complete explanation of the 95% K⁺ result requires considering electrical charge balance: if only K⁺ can cross and no compensating charge movement occurs, an opposing membrane potential can prevent K⁺ concentrations from nearly equalizing. This omission does not change the intended conclusion that K⁺ channels selectively facilitate K⁺ transport.
